I read the current default calibration of the real IQM Garnet computer. It is calibration set 9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d, measured at 16:38 UTC on 2026-10-22. It lists an IRB fidelity for each of the 30 CZ pairs. I checked every chain of 3 connected qubits a-b-c and multiplied the two CZ fidelities in each chain.

The best chain is QB11-QB12-QB7, with QB12 in the middle. The QB11-QB12 CZ has fidelity 0.999454. The QB12-QB7 CZ has fidelity 0.999066. Their product is 0.998520. The runner-up is QB11-QB12-QB17, with a product of 0.998175.

I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly those qubits. QB12 is rotated into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Two CZ gates, QB12-QB11 and QB12-QB7, then copy that state onto the outer qubits. Each CZ has single-qubit rotations around it. I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots and measured all 3 qubits. The job ID is 01a16482-a270-72dc-afdd-16fc0c47a676, and it completed. I read the circuit back from the server. It has exactly 2 CZ gates, and it measures QB11, QB12 and QB7.

The counts were 000: 49, 011: 51, 100: 51, 111: 49. A perfect quantum computer would give only 000 and 111, about half each. That is the GHZ principle: the three qubits are entangled, so they always agree with each other. These counts do not show it, because the mock service returns random results that do not depend on the circuit. I checked the circuit the server received with a noiseless simulation, and it gives 50% 000 and 50% 111. To see the real effect, the same circuit would need to run on real Garnet, which costs credits. Mock jobs cost 0 credits.
